course_title: Common and Specific Factors in Mental Health Treatments
course_description:
This course is designed to prepare you for clinical practice in the mental health field by critically engaging with key research, knowledge and skills relative to the common and specific factors paradigm. An emphasis is placed on how different therapeutic traditions conceptualise and manage different phases and tasks of treatment. The development of basic therapeutic skills required for effective therapeutic practice is also emphasised.

This course is designed to prepare you for clinical practice in the mental health field by critically engaging with key research, knowledge and skills relative to the common and specific factors paradigm. An emphasis is placed on developing basic therapeutic skills, on developing a procedural view of psychotherapy, and on learning how different therapeutic traditions conceptualise and manage the different therapeutic tasks.

course_aims:
1. Facilitate a reflective and critical approach to a procedural view of treatment and to the “common factors” paradigm in mental health treatments

2. Facilitate the learning of common therapeutic skills for mental health treatment

3. Facilitated the training of basic therapeutic skills relative to common factors approach and to relevant Art Therapy and Psychotherapy traditions

learning_outcomes.description: Recognise key concepts and critically review the common and specific factors paradigm in mental health treatments
Identify and differentiate how relevant Art Therapy and Psychotherapy traditions conceive the different phases of treatment and common factors in mental health treatment
Practice basic therapeutic skills relative to common factors approach and to relevant Art Therapy and Psychotherapy traditions

assessment_details.title: Lead tutorial discussion about a common factor
assessment_details.category: Participation/ Student contribution, Presentation, Tutorial/ Problem Set
assessment_details.task_description: In this activity you will present to the tutorial group a critical analysis of the arguments in favour and against recognising a given therapeutic task as a common factor across different therapeutic traditions. In this discussion, you will first present the arguments and evidence in favour of this claim, including evidence of its presence in two different therapeutic interventions. Then you will play the "Devil’s advocate" role and consider arguments against recognising this aspect of therapy as a ‘common factor’. Be mindful that that you might be asked to discuss a common factor that enjoys wide recognition, one that is emerging or is contentious: in these last cases you might need to infer or ‘read between lines’ to identify this factor within the therapeutic traditions you analyse. Your presentation should be clear, articulate and appealing, following post-graduate standards, citing or identifying authors or sources as necessary, to differentiate them from your own ideas. If you wish, you can use PowerPoint slides and other resources to support your presentation. The presentation will take up to 15 minutes. At the end of the presentation your tutor will lead a brief Q&A session with you to then pass to the open discussion with the tutorial group. At the start of the semester the tutor will decide with students the roster of presentations for the rest of the semester. Students should send the 'bare bones' of their presentation to the tutors or course coordinator one week before the presentation date to be checked, get feedback and support as needed. Approved materials for this assessment are the required readings. Any other reading needs to be approved by your tutor or course coordinator. The use of AI is allowed prior discussion with the tutor or course coordinator for purposes such as enhancing clarity of text, and surveying the existence of other valuable content, in which case it should be acknowledged during the presentation. Following UQ guidelines, this assessment will marked against a rubric available to students, and it will be recorded for eventual review purposes. Summarising, during your presentation you should: a) Identify and define the common factor you want to discuss. Brief history (if it’s already recognised as such), it's clinical relevance and supporting research. b) Present the arguments in favour of this common factor, analysing how it manifests it two distinctive traditions. c) Present the arguments against considering this therapeutic task as a common factor. d) Present a clear, well organised, articulate and visually appealing presentation (you might use PowerPoint slides), respecting the 10-15 minutes for the presentation and the following 10-minute Q&A session. The exact duration of the presentation will be determined and communicated by the tutor (based on the number of students presenting on the same day). assessment_details.title: Application of a common factor into your clinical practice
assessment_details.task_description: As we have seen through the semester, common factors are conceptualised and practiced differently across various therapeutic traditions. For this assessment, you will present a clinical vignette from your own clinical practice in which you apply one of the common factors discussed in this course, including the impact this intervention had over the client. You will then discuss how the particular way in which you practice this common factor might reflect a particular therapeutic tradition you practice and identify with, and then reflect on the benefits and disadvantages of the way you conceive and practiced this common factor compared to how its conceived and practice by an alternative tradition. Even though AI use is permitted, the focus of this assessment is your capacity to analyse knowledge, reflect and demonstrate independent thinking. The use Artificial Intelligence (AI) for the essay should be appropriately acknowledged in the references. Following UQ guidelines, this assessment will marked against a rubric that will be available for students. In summary: 1. Provide a clinical vignette of a case demonstrating the use of a common factor, including the effect this intervention had over the client, explaining how you came to this conclusion. 2. Identify the therapeutic tradition that informs the way you practice this common factor, explaining how you came to this conclusion, and explaining how this relates with your previous training and/or identity as therapist.. 3. Reflect on the benefits and disadvantages of the way you practice this common factor compared to how its conceived and practice by an alternative tradition. 4. Essay is written at a postgraduate level; referencing and citation follow standard format and the word count adheres to limit (excluding references) with +/- 10% tolerance. learning_activities.topic: T1: Introduction to the Course Review of Course Profile with students, including learning objectives, activities, learning method, and assessment pieces for the course. Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

T2: The Dodo verdict and the common factors paradigm Discussion of readings that explore the common factors paradigm and alternative views. Are all therapies equally effective/efficacious? Can common and specific factors be teased apart? Are specific therapies and traditions obsolete? Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Workshop 1: Process and stages of change. Common factors theory Workshop 1: What is psychotherapy, which are its main traditions, and how does it work? Process and stages of treatment. Common factors theory (theoretical) Delivered by Dr Jaime Yasky Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Learning outcomes: L01, L03

Workshop 2: Building therapeutic alliance Workshop 2: Building therapeutic alliance: bond, task and goals (theory - skills) Delivered by Mr Sam McArdle Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Learning outcomes: L01, L03

Workshop 3: Using mindfullness to enhance common factors Workshop 3: Other common factors: empathy, facilitation of emotional experience, genuineness/congruence, appreciation, non-judgmental attitude (theory - skills) Delivered by Dr Jaya Judd Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Learning outcomes: L01, L03

T3: Procedural view and dose of treatment Discussion of readings that explore the process view of therapy and related issues. Different approaches to phases of treatment and stages of change. Do therapeutic processes have a distinctive shape and critical stages? The dose effect: the more the merrier or is the quicker the better? What is the cost-effectiveness argument? Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

T4: The therapeutic alliance Discussion of readings that explore the origin and alternative views of the therapeutic alliance. Working alliance, therapeutic relationship, transference and real relationship: are they the same? Is having an emotionally corrective experience inherent to the therapeutic alliance? Can good alliance oppose therapeutic gain? Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

T5: Client factors, feedback and responsiveness Importance of client factors. Discussion of readings that explore factors from the client and the therapist affecting therapeutic process and outcome. Is the client always right? What are the benefits and perils of accommodating to the clients characteristics and preferences? Therapists responsiveness and use of feedback. How do we know how the client is doing? What are the pros and cons of feedback measures? What are the advantages and disadvantages of being responsive to the client? Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

T6: Different platforms for the 'talking' cure Discussion of readings that explore modalities of therapy that rely on alternative communication / interaction platforms (play, art, movement, drama, music, writing, etc.) Does therapeutic change require a talking modality of treatment? In what conditions are other communication / interaction modalities of treatment needed and beneficial? What is it that cures? Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

T7: Validation (support) vs Challenge (exploration/confrontation) in therapy Discussion of readings that explore the use and aims of supportive and of exploratory interventions. What kind of changes happen in therapy? Is therapy about returning to 'normal' or about undergoing a transformative experience? Is therapy a haven of unconditional acceptance or a place to be challenged? Are these two emphases found in all types of therapies? Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

T8: Support preparing for application of a common factor essay Session aimed at support students with preparing their written essay. Students are meant to bring their chosen common factor, their clinical vignette and draft of analysis/discussion to get feedback and support with any challenge they are facing with the preparation of this essay.

T9: Therapy as a skills building instance Preparing for what life throws at you. Discussion of readings that explore the idea of therapy as a skills development instance. What are the advantages and disadvantages of conceiving therapy as a skills training instance? Explicit and implicit teaching of skills: In what different ways are skills taught in therapy? Do all therapies (explicitly or implicitly) teach skills? Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

T10: Mentalizing, perspective taking, changing thinking and meaning making Flexing your thinking and seeing things differently. Discussion of readings that explore change in mentalising, thinking or in meaning as key task in therapy. How important is processing and resignifying experience, changing perspective and beliefs for the therapeutic process? In what different ways can this happen? Do these concepts (mentalizing, resignifying, mental processing, cognitive restructuring, perspective taking, etc.) refer to the same or to different things? Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

T11: Changing maladaptive patterns Acknowledging our contribution to vicious cycles or karma. Discussion of readings that explore the importance of awareness and self-control to change pathological patterns (behavioural, intrapsychic and interpersonal). How important is insight to change self-defeating habits? What's the role of being accountable for, owning and mastering our behaviour to change toxic habits? Is insight indispensable for change? Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Art therapy only: Eren,N et al (2014) Psychosocial, symptomatic and diagnostic changes with long-term psychodynamic art psychotherapy for personality disorders, The Arts in Psychotherapy 41 :375 385 Learning outcomes: L01, L02

T12: Exposure, distress tolerance and change Challenging avoidance, facing and sitting with distress. Discussion of readings that explore the importance of connecting with problems and associated distress as an essential task in therapy. How important is exposure for change? Is exposure an internal or external process or experience? Again, is therapy a haven or a place to face our demons? What are different forms of In session and out of session exposure? Please refer to ‘Learning Resources \\ Course Reading List’ for this session’s compulsory readings. Learning outcomes: L01, L02
